clue.text: Takes off faster, so leaves behind …

definitions.meaning: read playfully: removes clothes more quickly than someone else
gets ahead of and leaves trailing

explanation.surface: A sprinter's quick getaway leaves rivals behind, the clue trailing off into the next across clue.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links this clue to 6 across but adds nothing to the wordplay. The first reading splits the word as OUT- (more than) plus STRIPS (undresses).
explanation.definitionFit: To outpace rivals is to leave them behind, and the word also reads as undressing more quickly than another.

clue.text: Foot slipped going round bend? If a car crashed, it's one of 26 22 down's

indicators.note: going round says the shuffled letters surround the next piece
slipped suggests the letters of foot slide out of order

parts.note: a U-bend, so U stands for a bend

indicators.note: crashed signals the letters of these words smashed into a new order

explanation.surface: A driver's foot slips on a bend and the car crashes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going round' puts U, a U-bend, inside the result of 'slipped'; 'crashed' shuffles the letters of 'If a car'. The question mark covers the cheeky 'bend' for U.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1985 Karen Blixen film whose Oscar-winning soundtrack was by the composer JOHN BARRY.

clue.text: Frozen scene able to be negotiated by Greek character

indicators.note: a word negotiated by another is passed through by it, so it sits inside

parts.note: tau is a letter of the Greek alphabet

explanation.surface: A frozen scene can be bargained over by a Greek.
explanation.definitionFit: A tableau is a group of motionless figures representing a scene, as on stage.

clue.text: 22 down 26 scores, when starting regularly in games

indicators.note: in says that letter goes inside the word for games

parts.note: ties are matches, as in cup ties

indicators.note: starting picks out the first letter of the word regularly

explanation.surface: A rugby player scores when he starts regularly in matches.
explanation.walkthrough: 22 down 26 is BARRY JOHN, the Welsh rugby player, whose scores include tries.
explanation.definitionFit: In rugby a try is scored by grounding the ball over the opponents' line.

clue.text: Having cover pulled up from under us, nightly

indicators.note: pulled up says the hidden letters are read backwards
the clue word that says the letters sit inside the next words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A protective cover is yanked from under people each night.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'pulled up' reads upwards, so DERUSNI, hidden 'from' under us, nightly, is reversed.
explanation.definitionFit: Being insured means holding a policy that provides cover against loss.

clue.text: Sat around near small cafe, lacking a place for formal occasions

indicators.note: near says the first piece sits beside the next
around suggests the letters of sat are turned about into a new order
lacking means the letter a is removed

parts.note: a tearoom is a small cafe serving tea

explanation.surface: Someone lounged near a little cafe, missing a proper venue for formal events.
explanation.walkthrough: 'around' rearranges 'Sat', and 'near' simply places it beside the cafe; 'lacking a' takes one A from the tearoom.
explanation.definitionFit: A stateroom is a grand room used for ceremonies and formal receptions, as in a palace.

clue.text: … one of 26 22 down's daughters, starting to head out of Czech city

indicators.note: starting points to the opening letter of the word daughters
head out of says the first letter of the city's name is dropped

parts.note: Brno is the second city of the Czech Republic

explanation.surface: Continuing 1 across: someone's daughters set off from a Czech city, leaving others behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 26 22 down is JOHN BARRY, the film composer, who arranged the James Bond theme for the first Bond film.
explanation.definitionFit: The first James Bond film, for which the composer arranged the famous theme music.

clue.text: Flower girl and criminal

indicators.note: criminal suggests the letters of these words are bent out of shape

explanation.surface: A girl selling flowers keeps company with a crook.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flower' means something that flows, a river: the Darling is in Australia.
explanation.definitionFit: The Darling is a major Australian river, and a river is a crossword flower since it flows.

clue.text: Essential scenes shot before virgin blows top

indicators.note: before puts the first piece ahead of the second
shot suggests the letters of scenes are broken up and rearranged
blows top means the first letter is lost

parts.note: the Virgin Mary

explanation.surface: Filming scenes before a pure innocent loses their temper is vital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shot' shuffles SCENES into NECESS; MARY 'blows top' to give ARY.
explanation.definitionFit: Necessary means needed or indispensable, the same as essential.

clue.text: Second fattest short bottles of beer

indicators.note: short means the word loses its final letter

parts.note: tubbiest means fattest, most rotund

explanation.surface: Someone drinks beer from small bottles and is second fattest in the room.
explanation.definitionFit: Stubbies are short squat beer bottles, a name especially common in Australia.

clue.text: See 1 down
Pudding in place for tea, we hear

indicators.note: we hear says the phrase is to be spoken, giving a word that sounds like it

parts.note: the letter T (tea) has its place in the alphabet following the letter S, spoken as ess

explanation.surface: A pudding is served in place of the evening meal called tea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tea' is the letter T, whose place in the alphabet is after S; said aloud, 'after S' gives the word. In Britain 'tea' can mean an evening meal, which sells the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Afters is informal British for the dessert course that follows the main meal.

clue.text: Start off with most voracious appetite, being extremely tall and thin?

indicators.note: start off says the opening letter of the word is removed

parts.note: greediest means having the most voracious appetite

explanation.surface: A tall thin person turns out to have the biggest appetite of all.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks a playful definition: reeds are tall and thin, so the most reed-like is extremely so.
explanation.definitionFit: Reedy describes something slender like a reed, so the superlative means thinnest and lankiest of all.

clue.text: Get the fruit of another's labour? That's a feature of 22 down 26's game plan, initially

definitions.text: Get the fruit of another's labour?

parts.note: 22 down 26 is BARRY JOHN, the Welsh rugby player, and the scrum is a set piece of rugby

indicators.note: initially picks out the first letter of the word plan

explanation.surface: Taking credit for another's work is likened to part of a sports star's tactics.
explanation.walkthrough: BARRY JOHN was a celebrated Welsh rugby fly-half of the 1970s.
explanation.definitionFit: To scrump is British slang for stealing apples from an orchard, literally taking fruit someone else grew.

clue.text: (300+10)/¼ = score from free play?

indicators.note: the slash read as divided by: one numeral group is split open by another

parts.note: CCC is 300 in Roman numerals
1/4 in British date notation is 1 April, APR I
the digits 1 and 0 read as the letters I and O

explanation.surface: An arithmetic sum promises to equal the score from a free play.
explanation.walkthrough: The '/' means 'divided by': APR I splits the Cs. British dates put the day first, so 1/4 is 1 April.
explanation.definitionFit: A capriccio is a lively musical piece in free form, so a score written as a kind of free play.

clue.text: 22 down 26 scores one steel pan arrangement

indicators.note: an arrangement in music reworks a piece, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A rugby star scores with a steel pan arrangement, as if in a Caribbean band.
explanation.walkthrough: BARRY JOHN, the Welsh fly-half, also kicked these.
explanation.definitionFit: Penalty kicks at goal score points in rugby, a fly-half's stock in trade.

clue.text: 22 down 26's trademark wild dog and polar bears

indicators.note: wild suggests the letters of the two animal words run free into a new order

explanation.surface: A sportsman's signature involves a wild dog and some polar bears.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bears' is a link word, meaning the wordplay carries the answer. BARRY JOHN, the Welsh rugby fly-half, was famed for kicking these.
explanation.definitionFit: A rugby fly-half's signature move: a goal scored by drop-kicking the ball over the bar.

clue.text: Good-for-nothing actor providing new content for Sun's gaps in layout?

indicators.note: new content says the inside of the next word is swapped for something else

parts.note: the word Sun's read as SUNS, keeping its outer letters

indicators.note: read literally: G (good) put in place of O (nothing, zero)

parts.note: Al Pacino is the American film actor

explanation.surface: A worthless actor is hired to fill gaps in a tabloid newspaper's page layout.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Good-for-nothing' is read literally, G in place of O, on Al Pacino's surname; 'providing new content for' replaces the middle of Sun's. The Sun is a British tabloid newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: Spacings are the gaps left between letters, words or lines when a page is laid out.

clue.text: Place in Bond film — one of 26 22 down's

indicators.note: in puts that abbreviation inside the next word

parts.note: a chain is a bond or fetter

explanation.surface: A spot in a James Bond film is linked to a composer's work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bond film' pulls towards 007, but Bond is CHAIN and film the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1992 biopic of the silent star, whose soundtrack was by the composer JOHN BARRY.

clue.text: Windows feature in mirror (a bed isn't in reflection)

indicators.note: in reflection says the hidden letters are read backwards
the clue word that says the letters sit inside the next words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A mirror shows a bed that is not actually there, being only a reflection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' marks the letters held in the clue text, and 'in reflection' turns RABEDIS round.
explanation.definitionFit: A sidebar is a panel at the side of a computer screen or window, as in Microsoft Windows.

clue.text: Just in, without a break, for one-month try-out

definitions.text: Just in, without a break, for one

parts.note: Mar is the abbreviation for March

indicators.note: out signals the letters of try are put out of order

explanation.surface: A new arrival gets a month's trial with no break.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Just in, without a break' joins up as JUSTIN: Justin Martyr was a second-century saint, so he is one example of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Saint Justin is known as Justin Martyr, executed for his faith, so he is an instance of such a person.

clue.text: Liqueur drunk at a fair

indicators.note: drunk suggests the letters of these words reel into a new order

explanation.surface: Liqueur is drunk at a fair.
explanation.definitionFit: Ratafia is a liqueur flavoured with almonds or fruit kernels.

clue.text: Put out of action by baddies running round lake

indicators.note: round says the shuffled letters go around the next piece
running suggests the letters of baddies move about into a new order

explanation.surface: Villains racing around a lake have been put out of action.
explanation.walkthrough: 'running' shuffles BADDIES into DISABED, which goes 'round' L.
explanation.definitionFit: Something disabled has been rendered inoperative or incapacitated.

clue.text: Trouble as one taking orders runs away

indicators.note: away says the letter for runs is taken out

parts.note: a brother is a monk or friar, who takes holy orders
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: There is trouble when a waiter or junior taking orders runs off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taking orders' suggests a waiter, but it means taking holy orders.
explanation.definitionFit: Bother means trouble or fuss, as in 'it was no bother'.

clue.text: One who scored piece of music found in front of unsigned library book

indicators.note: found in front of places the bar ahead of what follows

parts.note: a bar is a short measure of music

indicators.note: unsigned means a sign of the zodiac, Libra, is taken away

parts.note: John is a book of the New Testament

explanation.surface: A composer found a sheet of music in front of an unsigned book from the library.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One who scored' suggests the composer John Barry, but this BARRY JOHN is the Welsh rugby fly-half who scored points.

clue.text: Fair chance of taking time out from equestrian competitions?

indicators.note: out from says the letter for time is removed from the word

parts.note: horse trials are called events, as in three-day eventing

explanation.surface: Riders taking a break from horse trials wonder about their chances.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taking' is a link word here.
explanation.definitionFit: Evens are betting odds of one to one, a fifty-fifty chance.

clue.text: Recalled sickly green eyespots on peacock

indicators.note: recalled, called back, says the two pieces are read backwards

parts.note: sickly means ill
eco is a short form meaning environmentally green

explanation.surface: Someone remembers a nauseous green colour in a peacock's tail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Recalled' reverses ILLECO.
explanation.definitionFit: Ocelli are eye-like spots of colour, the circular markings on a peacock's tail feathers.

clue.text: Robben half-heartedly upset with ref giving score by 26 22 down

indicators.note: upset tells us the letters of the combined words are overturned into a new order
half-heartedly removes one of the two letters at the heart of Robben

explanation.surface: Dutch footballer Arjen Robben, half-hearted and upset with the referee, scores.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half-heartedly' drops one of Robben's middle Bs to give ROBEN; 'upset' shuffles ROBEN plus REF. JOHN BARRY wrote the music for the 1966 lion film.
explanation.definitionFit: The film about Elsa the lioness, whose Oscar-winning music and title song were written by this composer.

Soft form of sunlight featuring in Laurel's beauty treatments
